processing: Naturally trained bushes are shaded under trellises covered with rice straw for about 20 days, light being reduced in stages, and picked by hand. The leaf is then processed as gyokuro.
harvest_season: Spring, picked by hand after the straw shading.
appearance_dry: Fine, dark, glossy green needles, as is typical of top gyokuro.
appearance_liquor: Pale green-gold and clear, with a thick feel.
appearance_wet: Soft, even, deep green shoots, a sign of hand-picking.
taste_profile: Rich, deep umami and mellow body, with the characteristic shaded aroma known as ōika.

brewing.notes: Typical gyokuro settings. Keep the water cool and the cup small; do not rush the first steep. Hotter water wastes this tea.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year spring tea in small tins, with the GI mark on qualifying lots. Quantities are small and prices high because of the hand labour. Keep it sealed and cold and aim to drink it within about a year.
description:
This is the strict version of Yame gyokuro: a Geographical Indication limited to leaf from the hill country of Yame and neighbouring towns in Fukuoka, made by three old methods together. The bushes grow naturally trained rather than clipped, shade comes from rice straw on trellises and every shoot is picked by hand.

The method is slow. Straw goes on in stages for about 20 days before picking, and the near-darkness slows the leaf and builds its savoury compounds. Hand-picking takes only the soft part of each shoot, so the leaf comes out unusually even.

In the cup it is thick and brothy, closer to a light stock than to sencha. Use a small amount of water at around 50 C and let the first steep sit for a couple of minutes. The second is quick, and the third fades toward a gentler green.

When buying, look for the GI mark. Plenty of good gyokuro from Yame is made with synthetic shading or machine picking, and that is fine tea but not this one.
history:
Gyokuro production in Yame began in 1904, and the natural training, straw shading and hand-picking have been passed down since then. The Yame Traditional Hon Gyokuro Promotion Council is the registered producer body.

The tea entered Japan's Geographical Indication register on 22 December 2015, as registration number 5, and took the grand prize at the Nihoncha Award in 2016. Yame growers have also dominated the gyokuro section of the National Tea Competition, including the area prize each year since 2001.
